title: One bad record
outcome: A line of plain text in a JSON topic stopped a partition for six hours while the consumer crashed and restarted on it.

content.bookmark: A record that can never be processed must be moved aside to a dead-letter topic, with its details, so the partition behind it can move on.

check.prompt: A plain Java consumer meets a record its deserializer can't read. What happens?
options: poll throws RecordDeserializationException, and the consumer won't move past the record by itself
check.why: The exception carries the partition and offset. The application decides what to do: log it, send it to a dead-letter topic, and seek past it.

check.prompt: Does the Apache Kafka consumer client have a built-in dead-letter topic?
options: No; the application writes to a dead-letter topic itself
Yes, it is on by default
check.why: Kafka Connect (for sink connectors) and Kafka Streams have dead-letter settings. A plain consumer has none: you build it.

check.prompt: What does Kafka Streams do with a record it can't deserialize, by default?
options: Logs it and fails, stopping the application
Sends it to a dead-letter topic
check.why: The default handler is LogAndFailExceptionHandler. LogAndContinue skips, and errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name sends records to a dead-letter topic.

check.prompt: What stops bad records from being written in the first place?
options: Producers serializing with a schema, checked by a schema registry
check.why: Schemaless JSON enforces nothing, so any text can be written. A schema-based serializer refuses data that doesn't fit before it reaches the topic.

caseStudy.setting: A bank (fictional) streams card transactions as JSON to card.transactions. A fraud-scoring consumer reads them and flags suspicious ones within seconds. A support engineer occasionally sends test messages using the console producer.

events.what: A support engineer testing connectivity sends the text "hello test" to card.transactions with the console producer.
The fraud consumer that owns that partition crashes on the record, restarts from its committed offset, reads the same record, and crashes again, about once a minute for six hours.
A customer reports fraud on their card that was never flagged. Every transaction on that partition since 02:10 was unscored.

pipeline: Card systems · produce JSON transactions, no schema
Fraud consumer · JSON deserializer, crashes on any parse error
tasks: Why did one record stop a whole partition?
What should the consumer do with a record it can never process?

debrief.title: Why one record stopped a partition
text: A partition is read in order. The consumer can't skip a record by itself: it either processes it or the application moves past it deliberately.
The consumer crashed before committing, so each restart resumed at the same offset and met the same record. Every record behind it on that partition waited for six hours.
This is a poison record: retrying can never help, because the record itself is the problem.

debrief.title: Moving it aside
text: Catch the deserialization error. Write the raw bytes, with the topic, partition, offset and error, to a dead-letter topic. Then seek past the record and carry on.
Alert on anything arriving in the dead-letter topic, and give it an owner who inspects and, if right, replays.
Separate permanent failures (bad data: dead-letter now) from transient ones (a timeout: retry later, scenario 10).

debrief.title: Stopping it at the source
text: Producers serializing with a schema (Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry) can't write arbitrary text.
Restrict who may write to production topics with ACLs, so test messages go to test topics.

takeaway: A poison record never succeeds on retry.
Dead-letter it with its context and move on, then alert.
Schemas and ACLs keep bad records out.
content.honesty: If you haven't handled poison records, say so and explain the pattern. If you have, say how you found the record and what you changed.

debrief.title: Questions
text: "What happens to all the other transactions when one is unreadable?"
"Who can write to the production topic?"

debrief.title: Requirements
text: One unreadable record never stops scoring for others; it is set aside and alerted within minutes.
Only the card systems can write transactions to production.

sayIt.question: How would you make sure one bad message can't stop a critical stream?
points: Name the risk: an unreadable message blocks everything behind it.
Require that bad messages are set aside to a dead-letter topic.
Require an alert and an owner for set-aside messages.
Require schemas so bad data is refused at the source.
Require write access only for the real producers.

tasks: What is the impact on customers?
What would you report to risk?

debrief.title: Customers
text: Rescore every unscored transaction from the gap, contact customers with confirmed fraud, and reimburse under policy.

debrief.title: Risk
text: Six hours of transactions unscored on one partition: report the window, the count and the fix to the risk owner.

sayIt.question: A control like fraud scoring silently stopped for part of the traffic. How do you handle it?
points: Scope the gap: which transactions, which hours.
Rescore and act on what was missed.
Report honestly to the risk owner.
Add monitoring of the control's coverage, not just its health.
Fund the prevention.

tasks: How do you run the incident?
What changes in access and process?

debrief.title: Running it
text: Move the consumer past the record (seek or a reset of that partition's offset by one), rescore the backlog, then deploy the dead-letter handling.

debrief.title: Access and process
text: No test messages on production topics; a test topic and ACLs that enforce it.
An alert for repeated consumer restarts.

sayIt.question: A consumer is crash-looping on one message. What do you do?
points: Find the partition and offset from the error.
Unblock: move past the record deliberately, keeping a copy.
Process the backlog behind it.
Add dead-letter handling and an alert.
Close the gap that let the bad record in.

tasks: How do you implement the dead-letter path?
How would it differ in Connect or Streams?

debrief.title: In a plain consumer
text: Catch RecordDeserializationException, read its partition and offset, produce the raw bytes and error details to card.transactions.dlq, seek to offset plus one, continue.
Commit after the dead-letter write succeeds, so a crash doesn't lose the bad record.

debrief.title: In Connect and Streams
text: Connect sink connectors: errors.tolerance=all with errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name and context headers.
Streams: errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name with the default handlers, or LogAndContinue to skip.

sayIt.question: How do you handle poison records in Kafka?
points: A poison record fails every time; retrying blocks the partition.
Plain consumer: catch the deserialization error, write it with context to a dead-letter topic, seek past.
Connect and Streams have dead-letter settings; the plain client doesn't.
Alert on and own the dead-letter topic.
Prevent with schemas and write ACLs.
